title: Roundup #86: Unintended consequences
gist: A nine-item roundup organized around 'unintended consequences': MAGA media audiences are collapsing as the movement built no lasting institutions, the falling US labor share may be substantially a tax-accounting illusion, high-skilled immigration and AI are each creating jobs rather than destroying them (OPT visas, Indian outsourcing), harm-reduction drug policy flooded American downtowns with disorder, and the current productivity boom looks driven by capital utilization from the AI investment wave rather than AI itself boosting output.

themes.theme: The MAGA media wave is breaking

insights.claim: Audiences for prominent MAGA influencers are falling sharply: Benny Johnson's YouTube views are down by millions from their 2024 peak, Nick Fuentes is trending down after gains in 2025 and early 2026, and outlets like The Blaze and The Federalist have seen even larger declines.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A measurable, trackable decline in right-wing media reach and engagement that signals waning grassroots MAGA intensity ahead of future elections and legislative fights.
insights.quote: It seems that everyone in the space is experiencing a drop-off in views from 2025
insights.locator: Here are some more details from the NYT

insights.claim: Noah Smith argues MAGA is a wave that will break and recede because the movement has built no lasting institutions — no civic groups, no religious revival, no professional associations, no governmental institutions — making it a pure populist rage movement that historically doesn't last.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A structural, institution-based argument for why current MAGA political dominance should be treated as cyclical rather than a durable realignment when modeling US political risk.
insights.quote: The movement has built no lasting institutions — no civic groups, no religious revival, no professional associations, no governmental institutions, nothing.
insights.locator: I've long predicted that MAGA is a wave

insights.claim: Trump's Iran war split a voter base that thought it was voting against Middle Eastern wars, his tariffs made the inflation he was elected to fix worse, and his only delivered promise — reduced immigration — hasn't materially improved most Americans' lives, all accelerating the movement's decline.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies specific, ongoing policy failures (Iran war, tariff-driven inflation) as the causal drivers of eroding Trump approval, useful for gauging durability of tariff and foreign-policy positions.
insights.locator: Trump's blunders, of course, have hastened the decline

insights.claim: A 'thermostatic effect' compounds the MAGA decline: people consume more partisan media when their party is out of power, so with Republicans controlling government there's less appetite for the ragebait media that fueled the movement's rise.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general mechanism (thermostatic media consumption) that predicts partisan-media audience cycles will keep inverting with control of government, useful for modeling media and advertising demand.
insights.locator: add the typical thermostatic effect

insights.claim: Noah Smith predicts popular unrest in America has peaked and is now declining, and that if the GOP throws off Trump's personality cult, the country may see 'one more round of crazy' (the DSA) before returning to more normal, productive politics.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A political-risk call worth tracking against actual election and policy outcomes: falling unrest would support a base case of de-escalating US domestic political volatility over the medium term.
insights.quote: this just strengthens my long-held view that popular unrest has actually peaked in America and is on the decline
insights.locator: Anyway, this just strengthens my long-held view

themes.theme: The falling labor share may be a statistical illusion

insights.claim: Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick argue much of the long, steady fall in labor's share of US income since 2000 may be a statistical illusion caused by tax-policy-driven reclassification of income rather than a real economic shift.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Challenges a foundational data series behind AI-job-loss and capital-redistribution narratives; if the labor share decline is overstated, related policy responses may be less urgent than assumed.
insights.locator: how a lot of the change you see on that graph might actually just be a statistical illusion

insights.claim: When a company converts from a C-corporation to an S-corporation, reported wages drop and reported profits jump because owners reclassify pay to avoid the 3.8% wage levy, and national accounts count S-corp profit as capital income; recharacterizing this reclassification raises the measured 2017 corporate labor share by about 0.9 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A precise, quantified correction (0.9pp) to the headline labor-share series driven by the 1986 Tax Reform Act's incentives, relevant to anyone using labor-share data as a macro or policy signal.
insights.quote: the corporate labor share in 2017 is about 0.9 percentage points higher
insights.locator: That change of label pulls down the measured labor share

insights.claim: Rising stock-based compensation for public-company employees generally doesn't show up as measured labor compensation; if roughly $200 billion of this 'missing' labor compensation were added back, it would explain about a third of the fall in the US labor share since the late 1970s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A second, sizable ($200B, ~1/3 of the decline) correction to the labor-share narrative rooted in how tech-heavy stock comp is measured — relevant to tech-sector labor-share and inequality debates.
insights.quote: If we could find around $200 billion of "missing" labor compensation, that would account for about a third of the fall in the labor share since the late 1970s.
insights.locator: A few years ago, Andrea Eisfeldt

insights.claim: Even after accounting for both the S-corp reclassification and stock-compensation measurement effects, a substantial portion of the fall in the US labor share remains unexplained, and further tax-driven distortions could shrink the real decline even more.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Counsels caution: the labor-share decline is real but probably smaller than headline figures suggest, so policy responses (capital redistribution, AI-jobs interventions) shouldn't be sized off the raw series.
insights.quote: This doesn't kill the idea that the falling labor share is a problem. But it's a warning that we need to figure out how big the problem really is
insights.locator: Even with both of these tax effects included

themes.theme: High-skilled immigration creates jobs for Americans

insights.claim: The Trump administration is reportedly considering charging foreign students a $100,000 fee to work in the US after graduation, reversing Trump's 2024 promise of automatic green cards for US university graduates and revealing that MAGA immigration policy targets high-skilled legal immigration, not just illegal immigration.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated policy proposal ($100K post-grad work fee) that would sharply raise the cost of hiring foreign STEM graduates in the US, relevant to tech and STEM-heavy employers' labor planning.
insights.locator: Trump's administration is reportedly considering charging

insights.claim: A study by Kwon, Lee, and Monras on the 2016 extension of the OPT program found that areas with more foreign STEM graduates saw firm creation rise by about 1%, native high-skilled employment rise by about 0.5 percentage points of the working-age population, and high-skilled native wages rise by about 1%, with no change in low-skilled employment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Hard, quantified evidence (firm creation +1%, native wages +1%) that restricting the OPT program Trump is targeting would likely reduce, not protect, native high-skilled American employment and wages.
insights.quote: the total number of firms [in an area that was allowed more OPTs] increased by approximately 1%…Native employment increased as well, by around 0.5 percent of the working-age population…high-skilled native wages increased by around 1%
insights.locator: A recent paper by Kwon, Lee, and Monras

insights.claim: High-skilled immigrants don't just compete with locals for a fixed pool of jobs; they lure investment into an area and expand the pool of jobs, an effect that more often than not outweighs the competitive effect and benefits native-born high-skilled workers most.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general economic mechanism investors can apply to any region or policy debate over skilled-visa restrictions: expect job-pool expansion effects to typically dominate direct competition effects.
insights.quote: if you let a bunch of foreign robotics engineers work in Pittsburgh, then a bunch of robotics companies are going to start up or open branch offices or factories in Pittsburgh
insights.locator: Note that the Americans who benefit most

themes.theme: AI is boosting rather than destroying Indian outsourcing

insights.claim: Despite widespread expectations that AI would devastate Indian back-office outsourcing firms, Indian service exports — heavily weighted toward the industries everyone expected AI to crush — are booming, per charts from economist Richard Baldwin.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A real-world counterexample to the AI-job-destruction narrative in a sector (BPO/outsourcing) considered maximally exposed, relevant for investors weighing AI disruption risk in services offshoring.
insights.locator: And Indian exports, which are heavily weighted

insights.claim: So far AI appears to be working as a complement to human labor rather than a substitute in the Indian outsourcing sector, though a future tipping point where AI flips to being a labor-replacer can't be ruled out.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A hedged, trackable thesis: current data supports an AI-complements-labor base case for outsourcing, but investors should watch for a discrete 'tipping point' shift toward substitution.
insights.quote: AI is working like a normal technology
insights.locator: the obvious answer is that AI is turning out

themes.theme: Harm-reduction drug policy has degraded American downtowns

insights.claim: Permissive 'harm reduction' drug policy in cities across the US and Canada, while including beneficial measures like naloxone distribution, also loosened restrictions on public drug use and led police to stop sweeping users and dealers from streets and parks, flooding downtown areas with drug users.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, reversible policy choice (public-use tolerance plus reduced policing) as the mechanism behind urban disorder in blue cities, informing municipal policy and urban real estate risk assessment.
insights.locator: this ended up flooding downtowns with drug users

insights.claim: From 2016 to 2025, 7,089 people died of drug overdoses in King County (Seattle), seven times the number of homicides in that period, even as harm-reduction policy proponents argued official injection sites reduce overdose deaths.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A stark, quantified public-health data point (7,089 deaths, 7x homicides) for assessing the real-world cost of harm-reduction policy in a specific major West Coast metro.
insights.quote: From 2016 to 2025, 7,089 people died of overdoses in King County, which includes Seattle—seven times the number of homicides in that period
insights.locator: Over the past decade, however, overdose-death rates climbed

insights.claim: Several major blue-city mayors are now quietly rolling back permissive harm-reduction policy: San Francisco's Daniel Lurie has ordered crackdowns on dealers and tent cities, Philadelphia's Cherelle Parker established a drug treatment court, San Jose increased policing and fines on negligent landlords, and Boston's Michelle Wu dropped injection-center plans and now emphasizes forced treatment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete, named list of city-level policy reversals worth tracking as leading indicators of whether blue-city urban disorder and downtown real estate distress will ease over the next few years.
insights.locator: As Powell notes, many blue cities are now quietly scaling

insights.claim: Noah Smith argues that letting downtowns become de facto reservations for drug users is a major reason America 'feels poorer' than European countries despite being materially richer, and serves as an anti-advertisement for progressive governance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Connects visible urban disorder directly to perceived US quality-of-life underperformance versus Europe, a framing relevant to urbanist policy and city-level real estate investment theses.
insights.quote: They are a big part of why America feels poorer than countries in Europe, even though it's actually a lot richer.
insights.locator: The article, which I strongly recommend reading

themes.theme: AI's contribution to the current productivity boom is unclear

insights.claim: Ernie Tedeschi finds that industry-level AI adoption bears little relation to recent productivity growth once pre-existing 2016-2019 productivity trends are stripped out — the sectors that adopted AI most heavily were already the ones with stronger pre-pandemic productivity growth, and the residual correlation falls to essentially zero.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the popular narrative that the recent US productivity acceleration is AI-driven, a key data point for investors pricing AI-adoption-linked equity premiums.
insights.quote: Strip out those pre-existing trends, and the residual correlation between AI adoption and recent productivity growth falls to essentially zero
insights.locator: Ernie argues that productivity growth doesn't seem to be concentrated

insights.claim: Tedeschi argues the recent acceleration in US labor productivity is instead being driven by 'macroproductivity' gains from the AI investment boom itself — companies running existing capital harder (longer factory runs, more server-rack and GPU-cluster utilization, more hotel occupancy) rather than AI directly making work more efficient.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI productivity story as a capex/capital-utilization phenomenon rather than an efficiency phenomenon — implies the productivity boost could fade once the investment boom itself levels off.
insights.quote: What appears to be lifting US labor productivity…are macroproductivity gains from AI…specifically companies running their existing capital harder.
insights.locator: In other words, this is all still early days

insights.claim: Supporting the bottleneck view, Suh et al. (2026) find that workers saving time with AI doesn't by itself make organizations more productive, Demirer et al. (2026) find engineers using AI to code faster don't end up shipping much more code, and Hill and Stein (2026) find AlphaFold's easier protein-structure prediction hasn't yet accelerated drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Three independent academic findings across coding, engineering, and drug discovery all showing AI time-savings failing to translate into higher output — a pattern-level bearish signal for near-term AI-driven productivity theses.
insights.locator: He cites Suh et al. (2026)

insights.claim: Botswana avoided the resource curse that afflicts most mineral-rich African countries by accumulating foreign-exchange reserves to stabilize its currency, running counter-cyclical budget surpluses and deficits, and investing diamond revenue in health and education, making it one of Africa's most successful economies.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A proven macro-policy playbook (FX reserves, counter-cyclical budgeting, human-capital investment) for resource-dependent economies, useful as a benchmark when evaluating other commodity exporters.
insights.locator: To prevent its currency from gyrating

insights.claim: Botswana's diamond production has fallen by more than half since 2022 as lab-grown diamond prices fall rapidly and gain share of the engagement-ring market, and the country's GDP per capita is now backsliding as a result.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete example of synthetic-diamond technology disrupting a real sovereign economy — relevant to anyone tracking lab-grown diamond adoption curves or natural-diamond miners' revenue exposure.
insights.locator: Botswana's diamond production has fallen by more than half since 2022

insights.claim: Economist Cesar Hidalgo notes Botswana's economic complexity has been trending downward for a while, showing it failed to translate its wealth and education investment into a diversified mix of more sophisticated sectors beyond diamond mining, illustrating that lasting national wealth comes from economic complexity and industrialization rather than natural-resource endowment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A cautionary case study for single-commodity economies (including Gulf petrostates, per Smith) that even well-managed resource wealth needs to be converted into diversified industrial capacity to be durable.
insights.quote: true lasting national wealth doesn't come from digging up rocks…True wealth comes from industrialization, not from control over natural resource deposits.
insights.locator: This is just one more reason

themes.theme: Interracial marriage patterns among US-born Americans

insights.claim: Among US-born newlyweds, most racial and ethnic groups show little gender asymmetry in interracial marriage: about 22% of Black men marry white women versus 18% of Black women marrying white men, and for Hispanics it's 29% versus 34%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Provides a quantified baseline debunking the common assumption that large race-gender marriage asymmetries are pervasive across US demographic groups.
insights.quote: About 22% of black men marry white women; about 18% of black women marry white men. For Hispanics it's 29% vs. 34%.
insights.locator: And the chart displays one overwhelming message

insights.claim: Chinese and Korean Americans are the major exceptions to the otherwise low gender gap in interracial marriage: only 18% of US-born Chinese American men marry white women versus 41% of Chinese American women, and 15% versus 40% for Koreans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Isolates two specific ethnic groups where a sharp, quantified gender asymmetry (roughly 2-3x) actually exists in the marriage data, contradicting a common narrative applied broadly across all groups.
insights.quote: Only 18% of U.S.-born Chinese American men marry white women, while 41% of Chinese American women marry white men. For Koreans, the gender ratio is similarly lopsided, at 15% to 40%.
insights.locator: However, there are two major exceptions

themes.theme: Nobody wants to read AI-generated writing

insights.claim: AI-generated content now accounts for about 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts, 13% of Reddit content, and 10% of Substack content, and on LinkedIn — where measurement is cleanest — AI-generated posts get 45% less engagement than human-written ones.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Hard, platform-specific data (41% of LinkedIn long-form content, -45% engagement) quantifying both the scale of AI content saturation and its measurable underperformance versus human writing.
insights.quote: AI now writes something like 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts, 13% of Reddit, 10% of Substack. And on LinkedIn, where the measurement is cleanest, AI-generated posts get 45% less engagement than human-written ones.
insights.locator: The numbers bear this out

insights.claim: The piece argues writing was never a supply problem, and that what's scarce is a specific person's judgment — having gone somewhere, noticed something, and being willing to be wrong about it in public — which AI's median, inoffensive output cannot substitute for.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A framework for content and media businesses: as AI text becomes commoditized and free, the economic value shifts entirely to scarce human judgment and voice, not volume of words produced.
insights.quote: What's still scarce is judgment: having gone somewhere, noticed something, and been willing to be wrong about it in public under your own name.
insights.locator: There's a supply-and-demand joke in here
